source_read: PDF pp. 581–589 (all pages; Figure 1, Tables 1–3 and Figure 2 checked on the rendered pages 583–586; Table 3 counts, P values and the editors' risk differences recomputed)

key_findings.note: Figure 1 (p. 583): 1267 assessed, 923 excluded, 344 randomized, 172 per arm; 5 placebo-arm participants not treated (3 no baseline visit, 1 incarcerated, 1 withdrew consent); 167 and 172 analysed, 0 excluded. Abstract › Results (p. 581) and Results › Participants (p. 584) agree.

Table 1 (p. 584): female 61 (36.5) + 65 (37.8) = 126; PHQ-9 of 10 or more 82 (49.1) vs 83 (48.3); injecting 81 (48.5) vs 74 (43.0); schooling median 10 (10–12). Results › Participants, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 584, continues p. 585): 179 (52.8%) unemployed (90 + 89 in Table 1), 136 (40%) prison history, mean 21 years of use, median 24 (17–28) days.

key_findings.correction: Every number confirmed (p. 585 text and Table 2): baseline 22.0 (20.3–23.8) and 23.1 (21.3–24.9); change −4.8 (−6.2 to −3.4) and −7.0 (−8.5 to −5.6); estimand −2.2 (−4.2 to −0.2), P = .02; IRR 0.89 (0.80–0.98); editors' 17.2 and 16.1 and the ratio-of-ratios check (0.697 / 0.782 = 0.89) recomputed. Only the attribution changes: the authors express the −2.2-day treatment estimand, not the rate ratio, as an 8% reduction in the risk of use on a given day (8 fewer use days per 100 possible days), and print the rate ratio in the same parenthesis. Suggested ending: '... treatment estimand −2.2 days (−4.2 to −0.2), P = .02, which the authors express as 8 fewer use days per 100 possible days; incidence rate ratio 0.89 (0.80 to 0.98).'

key_findings.note: p. 585, right column of the same paragraph: −1.3 (−3.3 to 0.6), P = .20; −1.9 (−3.9 to 0.1), P = .06; mean over 12 weeks −1.8 (−3.5 to −0.1), P = .03; robustness to imputation (eTable 7) and covariate adjustment (eFigure 2, eTables 8–9) stated, numbers only in Supplement 3.

key_findings.correction: Numbers confirmed (Table 2, p. 585), but the oral-fluid figure is not a week-12 value: oral fluid was compared across all three follow-up visits to give an average treatment estimand (Methods › End Points, p. 583; Statistical Analysis, p. 584); PHQ-9, AIS-5, HIV risk and EQ-5D are week-12 estimands. Suggested: 'Secondary end points, none significant: methamphetamine-negative oral-fluid samples averaged over weeks 4, 8 and 12, 12.0% (placebo) vs 13.2% (mirtazapine), difference 1.3 percentage points (−4.7 to 7.2), P = .68; at week 12, PHQ-9 change −0.2 (−1.3 to 1.0), P = .77; AIS-5 ...'. The same slip is in analysis.effect_sizes ('Secondary at week 12: methamphetamine-negative oral fluid ...').

key_findings.note: Figure 2 on the rendered p. 585: not depressed −2.8 (−5.7 to 0.0), depressed −1.4 (−4.2 to 1.4). Subgroup Analysis (p. 586): among people depressed at baseline, insomnia −1.8 (P = .001) at week 4, −1.7 (P = .002) at week 8 and −1.2 (−2.3 to 0.0; P = .04) at week 12; depression −1.2 (−2.8 to 0.5; P = .16) at week 12.
Every count and P value checked on the rendered Table 3. Editors' risk differences recomputed (Wald): drowsiness 13.6 (3.3 to 23.9), weight gain 6.9 (1.7 to 12.0).

Trial Design (p. 582); Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 583: 340 participants, 90% power, rate ratio 0.75, 75% follow-up, intervals not adjusted for multiplicity) and its last paragraph (p. 584: all analyses prespecified in the plan).

Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 587): 8% vs 14%; the attribution to a heterogeneous population, entrenched use, poor adherence and high discontinuation is in Strengths and Limitations (p. 587). The card's note (8% absolute, 11% relative from the IRR) recomputed.

reporting_issues.note: Abstract › Results (p. 581): positive mean difference of 2.2 days printed with the interval −4.2 to −0.2.

Substance confirmed (Results p. 585, Discussion p. 587; 1 − 0.89 = 11%). Page: the Introduction's description of the phase 2 result as a 14% difference is on p. 582 (Introduction, 3rd paragraph), so the page should read pp. 582, 585, 587.

Recomputed: 25/167 vs 40/172 gives P = .053 by uncorrected chi-square (.072 with continuity correction; .055 Fisher's exact), not .19. The uncorrected chi-square reproduces every other printed P value in Table 3 except one: suicide risk, 6/167 vs 5/172, printed .68 against .72 (.77 Fisher's exact). The card's phrase that the other P values match should exclude that row; trivial.

Abstract (p. 581): due to adverse events; Results (p. 584): reasons related to the trial medication; Table 3 (p. 586): due to adverse reactions; Figure 1 (p. 583): 29 vs 19 chose to stop (did not like the effects or felt it was not working), 10 vs 4 for adverse events or other health risks.
Table 1 (p. 584): EQ-5D utility median 0.92 (0.85–0.97) in both arms; Table 2 (p. 585): mean changes 1.3 and 2.2, estimand 0.9 (−3.1 to 4.9); no unit or rescaling stated.
Statistical Analysis (p. 583): estimands based on the 339 who received medication; Table 2 title (p. 585): intention-to-treat estimand.
11/339 = 3.2%, printed 4. Also trivial: the any-adverse-event total 300 (89) is 88.5%, which rounds to 88.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 is the right instrument and some concerns is the right overall judgment (never less severe than the worst domain). One domain-level disagreement (missing outcome data), which does not change the overall.

risk_of_bias_domains.note: No description of sequence generation or concealment in the article (pp. 582–583); balanced baseline (Table 1). RoB 2: 1.2 no information with 1.3 no gives some concerns.
Double-blind; the 5 excluded never attended the baseline visit or received medication, so their exclusion is unrelated to allocation (Figure 1).

Week-12 data for 293 of 339 (86%; 85% of the 344 randomized), which is not 'nearly all' for an estimate whose interval ends at −0.2 days (RoB 2 3.1 no). The mixed model and the multiple imputation both assume data missing at random, which RoB 2 does not accept as evidence that the result is unbiased (3.2 no); missingness could depend on use, since people using more may miss visits (3.3 probably yes); the similar proportions missing (12% vs 15%) make dependence not likely (3.4 probably no). The algorithm gives some concerns.
Self-reported primary outcome; drowsiness and weight gain could reveal allocation; no blinding check; the oral-fluid measure did not differ.
Registered, protocol published, all analyses stated as prespecified (pp. 582, 584); registry and plan not read, as the card says.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. Checked: the Key Points quotation is verbatim (10 words, p. 582); the Results call the null secondary results trends in favour (p. 585); Strengths and Limitations cites agreement of self-report with biological measures in this trial without discussing the null oral-fluid result (p. 587); the direct-effect inference is in the Discussion (p. 587). One addition: the abstract's Conclusions say mirtazapine reduced methamphetamine use (p. 581), causal wording for a self-reported outcome whose objective counterpart did not differ.

missed: Change versus level. The primary estimand is a difference in change from baseline. Because the mirtazapine arm began 1.1 days higher (23.1 vs 22.0, p. 585), the arms differ by only about 1.1 days at week 12 (16.1 vs 17.2, editors' calculation), half the 2.2-day estimand. The model enters baseline as one of the time points rather than as a covariate (Statistical Analysis, pp. 583–584), so part of the larger fall on mirtazapine could be regression from its higher baseline; the prespecified adjusted analysis uses covariates from the eligibility assessment, and its estimates are only in Supplement 3 (eFigure 2, eTables 8–9). Card and claim text that says '2.2 fewer days at week 12' should say a 2.2-day larger fall.

Correction notice: the PDF states that the article was corrected on 3 June 2026 to fix a misspelt author surname in the Visual Abstract (p. 581; Article Information, p. 587). It does not affect content, but METHODS §4.3 asks for corrections to be stored on the reference record, whose check reads clear.

Oral fluid also shows continued use: 86.8% and 88.0% of oral-fluid samples were not methamphetamine-negative (from 13.2% and 12.0% negative, Table 2, p. 585), which supports the card's point that most participants kept using.

Network context for the replication field: Coffin et al. (2020) shares no author with this trial (reference records), so the card's statement stands; its first author and Shoptaw are both authors of Trivedi et al. (2021), a bupropion trial (Bakouni et al., 2023, reference list), a link outside the mirtazapine trials.
